title: So God foreordained men's acts only by placing them in states and supplying aids and occasions, imposing no necessity
source_text: XXIX. Igitur non aliter volunt Deum praeordinavisse & praedefinivisse hominum actiones, quam quia voluit illos in eo statu creare, eaque agendi motiva auxilia, & occasiones iis subministrare, unde consequi praevidebat illos tali modo acturos, hasque potius quam illas volitiones elicituros esse; quanquam semper in eorum potestate maneret, vel sic, vel aliter agere; nulla nempe necessitate per omnia ista ipsis imposita, sic potius quam aliter agendi.
pass_a_gloss: XXIX. Therefore they will that God has preordained and predefined the actions of men in no other way, than because he willed to create them in that state, and to furnish them those motives, aids, and occasions of acting, from which he foresaw it would follow that they would act in such a way, and would elicit these rather than those volitions; although it always remained in their power, to act either thus, or otherwise; no necessity indeed being imposed on them through all those things, of acting thus rather than otherwise.
pass_b_english: They hold, therefore, that God preordained and predefined men's actions only in this sense: he willed to create them in that state and to supply them with the motives, aids and occasions for acting from which he foresaw that they would act in such a way and would produce these volitions rather than those.
All the while it remained in their power to act this way or otherwise, since none of these things imposed on them any necessity of acting this way rather than another.

lemmas.latin: non aliter volunt Deum praeordinavisse & praedefinivisse
lemmas.gloss: they will that God has preordained and predefined in no other way
motives, aids, and occasions of acting
it always remained in their power

choices.why: God's fixing an act beforehand by decree; 'predefine' keeps the Schools' term distinct from predetermination, and 'foreordain' renders praefinire where the authors use it as a synonym.
